name: ShadowKV (low-rank key cache on GPU, value cache offloaded)
bits: none by quantization; keys are compressed by a LOW-RANK representation and values are offloaded to CPU rather than reduced in precision.
activation_scheme: None. Stores the low-rank key cache on GPU and offloads the value cache, with an accurate KV selection strategy that reconstructs minimal sparse KV pairs on the fly to keep decoding latency low.
quality_delta: From the abstract: supports up to 6x larger batch sizes and boosts throughput by up to 3.04x on an A100 GPU without sacrificing accuracy, evaluated on RULER, LongBench and Needle-In-A-Haystack across Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3-8B-1M, GLM-4-9B-1M, Yi-9B-200K, Phi-3-Mini-128K and Qwen2-7B-128K.
notes: GROUP SIZE NOT APPLICABLE BY CONSTRUCTION: this scheme quantizes the KV cache, not the weights, so there are no weight groups to size. A number in this field would be a category error. (Where the underlying method has a real grouping - e.g. KIVI per-channel keys, KVQuant per-channel - that lives in the method's own record, not in weight_group_size.) Boundary record, and the one with the most interesting overlap with the rotation family: ShadowKV's low-rank key representation and QuaRot/SpinQuant's rotation-based approaches are both attacks on the fact that the key cache is highly redundant. Low rank says the redundancy is linear; incoherent rotation says it is an outlier problem. The paper's motivation is also a critique of prior sparse-attention work - that those methods either failed to cut GPU memory enough or paid significant decoding latency from CPU offloading - which is why the on-the-fly sparse reconstruction matters.
